maa11-wages.title: Wages, salary and overtime
maa11-wages.unit: Unit 1 – Consumer arithmetic, matrices and measurement
maa11-wages.coverage: Lesson concept checks followed by related subject revision.

questions.prompt: Wages, salary and overtime — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Overtime multipliers apply only to the stated overtime hours.
Every hour worked receives the overtime multiplier.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Overtime multipliers apply only to the stated overtime hours. Separate ordinary pay, overtime pay and allowances before adding. Applying the multiplier to all hours overstates earnings unless the contract explicitly says so.

questions.prompt: Pythagoras in two dimensions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Pythagoras requires perpendicular legs.
Pythagoras applies to every triangle.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Pythagoras requires perpendicular legs. Non-right triangles need another relation such as the cosine rule. Using a²+b²=c² without a right angle produces an unsupported length.

questions.prompt: Substitution and evaluating formulas — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Squaring t means multiplying t by itself, whereas 2t doubles it.
The t² term can always be replaced by 2t.
questions.explanation: Squaring t means multiplying t by itself, whereas 2t doubles it. The expressions agree only at particular values, such as 0 and 2. Replacing the power changes the formula and generally changes its predictions.

questions.prompt: Commission and piecework — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A 4% commission means the worker receives all sales plus another 4%.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Commission equals the eligible sales multiplied by the commission fraction, plus any stated base pay.
questions.explanation: Commission equals the eligible sales multiplied by the commission fraction, plus any stated base pay. Sales and wages are different quantities. Confusing them produces an implausibly large wage and makes comparisons invalid.

questions.prompt: Scale drawings, maps and units — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: The ratio first maps 1 cm to 10000 cm.
A 1:10000 map turns 1 cm into 10000 km.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: The ratio first maps 1 cm to 10000 cm. Convert that result to metres or kilometres afterward. Scale units must match before the ratio is used.

questions.prompt: Matrix cost models and compatible units — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Dimension compatibility is necessary but category alignment is also required.
Dimensionally compatible matrices always represent a meaningful cost calculation.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Dimension compatibility is necessary but category alignment is also required. Price and quantity columns must refer to the same products in the same order. A misplaced price can produce a mathematically valid but economically wrong total.

questions.prompt: Supplied allowance rules and payment periods — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Only income above the free area is reduced under this rule.
The reduction rate applies to all income even when a free-income area is supplied.
questions.explanation: Only income above the free area is reduced under this rule. Subtract the threshold first and apply the zero-payment floor last. Applying the reduction to the exempt portion understates the payment.

questions.prompt: Successive and reverse percentages — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Equal percentage increases and decreases always cancel.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Successive percentage changes multiply their factors.
questions.explanation: Successive percentage changes multiply their factors. A 10% rise then fall gives 1.1×0.9=0.99. Different reference amounts cause the failure to cancel; reverse an increase by division.

questions.prompt: Pythagoras and space diagonals — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A space diagonal is √(l²+w²+h²) for perpendicular edges.
The space diagonal is found by adding the three edge lengths.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: A space diagonal is √(l²+w²+h²) for perpendicular edges. Adding edges gives a route along boundaries, not a straight diagonal. Use two right triangles to justify the direct interior distance.

questions.prompt: Matrix addition and scalar multiplication — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Scalar multiplication changes every entry.
Multiplying a matrix by 2 changes only its diagonal entries.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Scalar multiplication changes every entry. The diagonal has no special exemption in scalar arithmetic. Scaling only part of a stock table understates the remaining delivery quantities.

questions.prompt: Circle sectors: arc, area and perimeter — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
A non-full sector perimeter includes the arc and its two radii.
The perimeter of a sector equals its arc length.
questions.explanation: A non-full sector perimeter includes the arc and its two radii. The curved boundary is only one part of the region’s edge. Omitting radial sides understates material needed for its complete boundary.

questions.prompt: Composite areas and boundary lengths — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Subtracting a pond area means its boundary must also be subtracted from all edging.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Area subtraction and boundary counting are different operations.
questions.explanation: Area subtraction and boundary counting are different operations. A pond reduces grass area but adds an exposed inner edge if edging is required there. Choose boundaries from the practical task rather than copying area signs.

questions.prompt: Spreadsheet models and absolute references — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Anchor shared constants and leave row-specific inputs relative.
Every reference in a fill-down formula should be absolute.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Anchor shared constants and leave row-specific inputs relative. Locking a changing hours reference repeats the first worker’s hours. Test both the first and final rows to check that fill-down follows the intended pattern.

questions.prompt: Unit costs and purchase decisions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Unit cost divides price by a standardised quantity.
The pack with the lowest sticker price always has the lowest unit cost.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Unit cost divides price by a standardised quantity. Different pack sizes can reverse the ranking of sticker prices. Compare whole-pack spending as well when a required quantity is given.

questions.prompt: Currency conversion and transaction fees — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The correct operation follows the rate’s units.
Multiply by the quoted rate in both conversion directions.
questions.explanation: The correct operation follows the rate’s units. Multiply AUD by foreign units per AUD; divide foreign units by that rate for AUD. Using multiplication in reverse gives the wrong amount and incompatible units.

questions.prompt: Matrix powers and multi-stage walks — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: An entry of A² automatically counts simple shortest paths.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Adjacency powers count walks with exactly the stated number of edges.
questions.explanation: Adjacency powers count walks with exactly the stated number of edges. Walks may repeat vertices and edges and ignore travel costs. Counting simple paths or shortest routes requires additional restrictions or a different method.

questions.prompt: Surface area and exposed faces — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Count only the exposed faces required by the task.
Every cylindrical object uses two end circles in a material-area calculation.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Count only the exposed faces required by the task. Open tops, labels and internal joins change the surface inventory. Using a closed-cylinder formula automatically can overestimate material.

questions.prompt: Area and volume under similarity — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Similar enlargement by k gives area factor k² and volume factor k³.
Doubling every length doubles both area and volume.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Similar enlargement by k gives area factor k² and volume factor k³. For k=2 the factors are 4 and 8. Confusing the powers greatly understates covering or capacity requirements.

questions.prompt: Personal budgets and cash-flow reserves — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Irregular bills need a reserve or another explicit funding plan.
Annual bills can be ignored because they are not paid every week.
questions.explanation: Irregular bills need a reserve or another explicit funding plan. Convert bills to the chosen budget interval before adding outflows. Omitting them overstates disposable income and can lead to a later cash shortfall.

questions.prompt: Composite solids and tank capacity — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A tank filled to 80% of its height is always 80% full by volume.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Height fraction equals volume fraction only for constant cross-sectional area.
questions.explanation: Height fraction equals volume fraction only for constant cross-sectional area. A cone or curved cap has changing area with height. Use the stated volume fraction directly or calculate the partial solid from its geometry.

The space diagonal is found by adding the three edge lengths.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: A space diagonal is √(l²+w²+h²) for perpendicular edges. Adding edges gives a route along boundaries, not a straight diagonal. Use two right triangles to justify the direct interior distance.

questions.prompt: Matrix addition and scalar multiplication — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

Scalar multiplication changes every entry.
Multiplying a matrix by 2 changes only its diagonal entries.
questions.explanation: Scalar multiplication changes every entry. The diagonal has no special exemption in scalar arithmetic. Scaling only part of a stock table understates the remaining delivery quantities.

questions.prompt: Circle sectors: arc, area and perimeter — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

A non-full sector perimeter includes the arc and its two radii.

questions.prompt: Composite areas and boundary lengths — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.

questions.prompt: Spreadsheet models and absolute references — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Unit costs and purchase decisions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Surface area and exposed faces — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Subtracting a pond area means its boundary must also be subtracted from all edging.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Area subtraction and boundary counting are different operations. A pond reduces grass area but adds an exposed inner edge if edging is required there. Choose boundaries from the practical task rather than copying area signs.

questions.prompt: Spreadsheet models and absolute references — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Anchor shared constants and leave row-specific inputs relative.
Every reference in a fill-down formula should be absolute.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Anchor shared constants and leave row-specific inputs relative. Locking a changing hours reference repeats the first worker’s hours. Test both the first and final rows to check that fill-down follows the intended pattern.

questions.prompt: Unit costs and purchase decisions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Unit cost divides price by a standardised quantity.
The pack with the lowest sticker price always has the lowest unit cost.
questions.explanation: Unit cost divides price by a standardised quantity. Different pack sizes can reverse the ranking of sticker prices. Compare whole-pack spending as well when a required quantity is given.

questions.prompt: Currency conversion and transaction fees — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Multiply by the quoted rate in both conversion directions.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The correct operation follows the rate’s units.
questions.explanation: The correct operation follows the rate’s units. Multiply AUD by foreign units per AUD; divide foreign units by that rate for AUD. Using multiplication in reverse gives the wrong amount and incompatible units.

questions.prompt: Matrix powers and multi-stage walks — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Adjacency powers count walks with exactly the stated number of edges.
An entry of A² automatically counts simple shortest paths.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Adjacency powers count walks with exactly the stated number of edges. Walks may repeat vertices and edges and ignore travel costs. Counting simple paths or shortest routes requires additional restrictions or a different method.

questions.prompt: Surface area and exposed faces — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Count only the exposed faces required by the task.
Every cylindrical object uses two end circles in a material-area calculation.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Count only the exposed faces required by the task. Open tops, labels and internal joins change the surface inventory. Using a closed-cylinder formula automatically can overestimate material.

questions.prompt: Area and volume under similarity — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Similar enlargement by k gives area factor k² and volume factor k³.
Doubling every length doubles both area and volume.
questions.explanation: Similar enlargement by k gives area factor k² and volume factor k³. For k=2 the factors are 4 and 8. Confusing the powers greatly understates covering or capacity requirements.

questions.prompt: Personal budgets and cash-flow reserves — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Annual bills can be ignored because they are not paid every week.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Irregular bills need a reserve or another explicit funding plan.
questions.explanation: Irregular bills need a reserve or another explicit funding plan. Convert bills to the chosen budget interval before adding outflows. Omitting them overstates disposable income and can lead to a later cash shortfall.

questions.prompt: Matrix cost models and compatible units — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Dimension compatibility is necessary but category alignment is also required.
Dimensionally compatible matrices always represent a meaningful cost calculation.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Dimension compatibility is necessary but category alignment is also required. Price and quantity columns must refer to the same products in the same order. A misplaced price can produce a mathematically valid but economically wrong total.

questions.prompt: Wages, salary and overtime — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Overtime multipliers apply only to the stated overtime hours.
Every hour worked receives the overtime multiplier.
questions.explanation: Overtime multipliers apply only to the stated overtime hours. Separate ordinary pay, overtime pay and allowances before adding. Applying the multiplier to all hours overstates earnings unless the contract explicitly says so.

questions.prompt: Pythagoras in two dimensions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Pythagoras applies to every triangle.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Pythagoras requires perpendicular legs.
questions.explanation: Pythagoras requires perpendicular legs. Non-right triangles need another relation such as the cosine rule. Using a²+b²=c² without a right angle produces an unsupported length.

questions.prompt: Substitution and evaluating formulas — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Squaring t means multiplying t by itself, whereas 2t doubles it.
The t² term can always be replaced by 2t.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Squaring t means multiplying t by itself, whereas 2t doubles it. The expressions agree only at particular values, such as 0 and 2. Replacing the power changes the formula and generally changes its predictions.

questions.prompt: Commission and piecework — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Commission equals the eligible sales multiplied by the commission fraction, plus any stated base pay.
A 4% commission means the worker receives all sales plus another 4%.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Commission equals the eligible sales multiplied by the commission fraction, plus any stated base pay. Sales and wages are different quantities. Confusing them produces an implausibly large wage and makes comparisons invalid.

questions.prompt: Scale drawings, maps and units — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The ratio first maps 1 cm to 10000 cm.
A 1:10000 map turns 1 cm into 10000 km.
questions.explanation: The ratio first maps 1 cm to 10000 cm. Convert that result to metres or kilometres afterward. Scale units must match before the ratio is used.

questions.prompt: Supplied allowance rules and payment periods — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: The reduction rate applies to all income even when a free-income area is supplied.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Only income above the free area is reduced under this rule.
questions.explanation: Only income above the free area is reduced under this rule. Subtract the threshold first and apply the zero-payment floor last. Applying the reduction to the exempt portion understates the payment.

questions.prompt: Successive and reverse percentages — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Successive percentage changes multiply their factors.
Equal percentage increases and decreases always cancel.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Successive percentage changes multiply their factors. A 10% rise then fall gives 1.1×0.9=0.99. Different reference amounts cause the failure to cancel; reverse an increase by division.

questions.prompt: Pythagoras and space diagonals — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
A space diagonal is √(l²+w²+h²) for perpendicular edges.
The space diagonal is found by adding the three edge lengths.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: A space diagonal is √(l²+w²+h²) for perpendicular edges. Adding edges gives a route along boundaries, not a straight diagonal. Use two right triangles to justify the direct interior distance.

questions.prompt: Matrix addition and scalar multiplication — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Scalar multiplication changes every entry.
Multiplying a matrix by 2 changes only its diagonal entries.
questions.explanation: Scalar multiplication changes every entry. The diagonal has no special exemption in scalar arithmetic. Scaling only part of a stock table understates the remaining delivery quantities.

options: The perimeter of a sector equals its arc length.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

A non-full sector perimeter includes the arc and its two radii.
questions.explanation: A non-full sector perimeter includes the arc and its two radii. The curved boundary is only one part of the region’s edge. Omitting radial sides understates material needed for its complete boundary.

questions.prompt: Surface area and exposed faces — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Every cylindrical object uses two end circles in a material-area calculation.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

questions.prompt: Area and volume under similarity — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.

Doubling every length doubles both area and volume.

questions.prompt: Personal budgets and cash-flow reserves — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Irregular bills need a reserve or another explicit funding plan.

maa11-matrixlanguage.title: Matrix information, order and special matrices
maa11-matrixlanguage.unit: Unit 1 – Consumer arithmetic, matrices and measurement
maa11-matrixlanguage.parent: Matrix information, order and special matrices

questions.prompt: Matrix information, order and special matrices — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Matrix order is rows first, columns second.
A 2×3 matrix has three rows and two columns.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Matrix order is rows first, columns second. A 2×3 array therefore has two rows and three columns. Reversing the order can make an invalid product appear valid and misidentify entries.

questions.prompt: Matrix cost models and compatible units — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Dimension compatibility is necessary but category alignment is also required.
Dimensionally compatible matrices always represent a meaningful cost calculation.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Dimension compatibility is necessary but category alignment is also required. Price and quantity columns must refer to the same products in the same order. A misplaced price can produce a mathematically valid but economically wrong total.

questions.prompt: Matrix addition and scalar multiplication — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

Scalar multiplication changes every entry.

questions.explanation: Scalar multiplication changes every entry. The diagonal has no special exemption in scalar arithmetic. Scaling only part of a stock table understates the remaining delivery quantities.

questions.prompt: Matrix powers and multi-stage walks — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: An entry of A² automatically counts simple shortest paths.

questions.prompt: Matrix multiplication: rows meet columns — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Matrix multiplication generally does not commute.
AB always equals BA because ordinary number multiplication commutes.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication generally does not commute. Reversing factors changes the row-column pairing and can even be dimensionally invalid. Choose the order from the labels and the desired output, not from a scalar rule.

questions.prompt: Wages, salary and overtime — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Overtime multipliers apply only to the stated overtime hours.
Every hour worked receives the overtime multiplier.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Overtime multipliers apply only to the stated overtime hours. Separate ordinary pay, overtime pay and allowances before adding. Applying the multiplier to all hours overstates earnings unless the contract explicitly says so.

questions.prompt: Pythagoras in two dimensions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Pythagoras requires perpendicular legs.
Pythagoras applies to every triangle.
questions.explanation: Pythagoras requires perpendicular legs. Non-right triangles need another relation such as the cosine rule. Using a²+b²=c² without a right angle produces an unsupported length.

questions.prompt: Substitution and evaluating formulas — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: The t² term can always be replaced by 2t.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Squaring t means multiplying t by itself, whereas 2t doubles it.
questions.explanation: Squaring t means multiplying t by itself, whereas 2t doubles it. The expressions agree only at particular values, such as 0 and 2. Replacing the power changes the formula and generally changes its predictions.

questions.prompt: Commission and piecework — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Commission equals the eligible sales multiplied by the commission fraction, plus any stated base pay.
A 4% commission means the worker receives all sales plus another 4%.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Commission equals the eligible sales multiplied by the commission fraction, plus any stated base pay. Sales and wages are different quantities. Confusing them produces an implausibly large wage and makes comparisons invalid.

questions.prompt: Scale drawings, maps and units — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The ratio first maps 1 cm to 10000 cm.
A 1:10000 map turns 1 cm into 10000 km.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: The ratio first maps 1 cm to 10000 cm. Convert that result to metres or kilometres afterward. Scale units must match before the ratio is used.

questions.prompt: Supplied allowance rules and payment periods — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Only income above the free area is reduced under this rule.
The reduction rate applies to all income even when a free-income area is supplied.
questions.explanation: Only income above the free area is reduced under this rule. Subtract the threshold first and apply the zero-payment floor last. Applying the reduction to the exempt portion understates the payment.

questions.prompt: Successive and reverse percentages — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Equal percentage increases and decreases always cancel.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Successive percentage changes multiply their factors.
questions.explanation: Successive percentage changes multiply their factors. A 10% rise then fall gives 1.1×0.9=0.99. Different reference amounts cause the failure to cancel; reverse an increase by division.

questions.prompt: Pythagoras and space diagonals — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A space diagonal is √(l²+w²+h²) for perpendicular edges.
The space diagonal is found by adding the three edge lengths.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: A space diagonal is √(l²+w²+h²) for perpendicular edges. Adding edges gives a route along boundaries, not a straight diagonal. Use two right triangles to justify the direct interior distance.

questions.prompt: Circle sectors: arc, area and perimeter — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
A non-full sector perimeter includes the arc and its two radii.
The perimeter of a sector equals its arc length.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: A non-full sector perimeter includes the arc and its two radii. The curved boundary is only one part of the region’s edge. Omitting radial sides understates material needed for its complete boundary.

questions.prompt: Composite areas and boundary lengths — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Area subtraction and boundary counting are different operations.
Subtracting a pond area means its boundary must also be subtracted from all edging.
questions.explanation: Area subtraction and boundary counting are different operations. A pond reduces grass area but adds an exposed inner edge if edging is required there. Choose boundaries from the practical task rather than copying area signs.

questions.prompt: Spreadsheet models and absolute references — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Every reference in a fill-down formula should be absolute.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Anchor shared constants and leave row-specific inputs relative.
questions.explanation: Anchor shared constants and leave row-specific inputs relative. Locking a changing hours reference repeats the first worker’s hours. Test both the first and final rows to check that fill-down follows the intended pattern.

questions.prompt: Unit costs and purchase decisions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Unit cost divides price by a standardised quantity.
The pack with the lowest sticker price always has the lowest unit cost.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Unit cost divides price by a standardised quantity. Different pack sizes can reverse the ranking of sticker prices. Compare whole-pack spending as well when a required quantity is given.

questions.prompt: Currency conversion and transaction fees — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The correct operation follows the rate’s units.
Multiply by the quoted rate in both conversion directions.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: The correct operation follows the rate’s units. Multiply AUD by foreign units per AUD; divide foreign units by that rate for AUD. Using multiplication in reverse gives the wrong amount and incompatible units.

questions.prompt: Composite areas and boundary lengths — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Currency conversion and transaction fees — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Surface area and exposed faces — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Equal percentage increases and decreases always cancel.

questions.prompt: Pythagoras and space diagonals — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
A space diagonal is √(l²+w²+h²) for perpendicular edges.
The space diagonal is found by adding the three edge lengths.
questions.explanation: A space diagonal is √(l²+w²+h²) for perpendicular edges. Adding edges gives a route along boundaries, not a straight diagonal. Use two right triangles to justify the direct interior distance.

questions.prompt: Matrix addition and scalar multiplication — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Multiplying a matrix by 2 changes only its diagonal entries.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Scalar multiplication changes every entry.
questions.explanation: Scalar multiplication changes every entry. The diagonal has no special exemption in scalar arithmetic. Scaling only part of a stock table understates the remaining delivery quantities.

questions.prompt: Circle sectors: arc, area and perimeter — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A non-full sector perimeter includes the arc and its two radii.
The perimeter of a sector equals its arc length.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: A non-full sector perimeter includes the arc and its two radii. The curved boundary is only one part of the region’s edge. Omitting radial sides understates material needed for its complete boundary.

questions.prompt: Composite areas and boundary lengths — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Area subtraction and boundary counting are different operations.
Subtracting a pond area means its boundary must also be subtracted from all edging.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Area subtraction and boundary counting are different operations. A pond reduces grass area but adds an exposed inner edge if edging is required there. Choose boundaries from the practical task rather than copying area signs.

questions.prompt: Spreadsheet models and absolute references — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Anchor shared constants and leave row-specific inputs relative.
Every reference in a fill-down formula should be absolute.
questions.explanation: Anchor shared constants and leave row-specific inputs relative. Locking a changing hours reference repeats the first worker’s hours. Test both the first and final rows to check that fill-down follows the intended pattern.

questions.prompt: Unit costs and purchase decisions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: The pack with the lowest sticker price always has the lowest unit cost.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Unit cost divides price by a standardised quantity.
questions.explanation: Unit cost divides price by a standardised quantity. Different pack sizes can reverse the ranking of sticker prices. Compare whole-pack spending as well when a required quantity is given.

questions.prompt: Currency conversion and transaction fees — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: The correct operation follows the rate’s units.
Multiply by the quoted rate in both conversion directions.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: The correct operation follows the rate’s units. Multiply AUD by foreign units per AUD; divide foreign units by that rate for AUD. Using multiplication in reverse gives the wrong amount and incompatible units.

questions.prompt: Matrix powers and multi-stage walks — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Adjacency powers count walks with exactly the stated number of edges.
An entry of A² automatically counts simple shortest paths.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Adjacency powers count walks with exactly the stated number of edges. Walks may repeat vertices and edges and ignore travel costs. Counting simple paths or shortest routes requires additional restrictions or a different method.

questions.prompt: Surface area and exposed faces — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Count only the exposed faces required by the task.
Every cylindrical object uses two end circles in a material-area calculation.

questions.prompt: Area and volume under similarity — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.

questions.prompt: Prisms, cylinders, cones and capacity — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

The cone volume is one third of that matching cylinder.
A cone has the same volume as a cylinder with the same base and height.

questions.prompt: Wages, salary and overtime — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Every hour worked receives the overtime multiplier.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Overtime multipliers apply only to the stated overtime hours.
questions.explanation: Overtime multipliers apply only to the stated overtime hours. Separate ordinary pay, overtime pay and allowances before adding. Applying the multiplier to all hours overstates earnings unless the contract explicitly says so.

questions.prompt: Pythagoras in two dimensions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Pythagoras requires perpendicular legs.
Pythagoras applies to every triangle.

questions.explanation: Pythagoras requires perpendicular legs. Non-right triangles need another relation such as the cosine rule. Using a²+b²=c² without a right angle produces an unsupported length.

questions.prompt: Substitution and evaluating formulas — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Squaring t means multiplying t by itself, whereas 2t doubles it.
The t² term can always be replaced by 2t.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Squaring t means multiplying t by itself, whereas 2t doubles it. The expressions agree only at particular values, such as 0 and 2. Replacing the power changes the formula and generally changes its predictions.

questions.prompt: Commission and piecework — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Commission equals the eligible sales multiplied by the commission fraction, plus any stated base pay.
A 4% commission means the worker receives all sales plus another 4%.
questions.explanation: Commission equals the eligible sales multiplied by the commission fraction, plus any stated base pay. Sales and wages are different quantities. Confusing them produces an implausibly large wage and makes comparisons invalid.

questions.prompt: Scale drawings, maps and units — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.

questions.prompt: Matrix cost models and compatible units — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Dimension compatibility is necessary but category alignment is also required.
Dimensionally compatible matrices always represent a meaningful cost calculation.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

questions.prompt: Wages, salary and overtime — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Overtime multipliers apply only to the stated overtime hours.
Every hour worked receives the overtime multiplier.
questions.explanation: Overtime multipliers apply only to the stated overtime hours. Separate ordinary pay, overtime pay and allowances before adding. Applying the multiplier to all hours overstates earnings unless the contract explicitly says so.

questions.prompt: Pythagoras in two dimensions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

Pythagoras requires perpendicular legs.

questions.prompt: Substitution and evaluating formulas — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Squaring t means multiplying t by itself, whereas 2t doubles it.
The t² term can always be replaced by 2t.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Squaring t means multiplying t by itself, whereas 2t doubles it. The expressions agree only at particular values, such as 0 and 2. Replacing the power changes the formula and generally changes its predictions.

questions.prompt: Commission and piecework — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Commission equals the eligible sales multiplied by the commission fraction, plus any stated base pay.
A 4% commission means the worker receives all sales plus another 4%.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Commission equals the eligible sales multiplied by the commission fraction, plus any stated base pay. Sales and wages are different quantities. Confusing them produces an implausibly large wage and makes comparisons invalid.

questions.prompt: Supplied allowance rules and payment periods — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Only income above the free area is reduced under this rule.
The reduction rate applies to all income even when a free-income area is supplied.
questions.explanation: Only income above the free area is reduced under this rule. Subtract the threshold first and apply the zero-payment floor last. Applying the reduction to the exempt portion understates the payment.

questions.prompt: Successive and reverse percentages — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Equal percentage increases and decreases always cancel.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Successive percentage changes multiply their factors.
questions.explanation: Successive percentage changes multiply their factors. A 10% rise then fall gives 1.1×0.9=0.99. Different reference amounts cause the failure to cancel; reverse an increase by division.

questions.prompt: Pythagoras and space diagonals — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

The space diagonal is found by adding the three edge lengths.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: A space diagonal is √(l²+w²+h²) for perpendicular edges. Adding edges gives a route along boundaries, not a straight diagonal. Use two right triangles to justify the direct interior distance.

questions.prompt: Matrix addition and scalar multiplication — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Scalar multiplication changes every entry.
Multiplying a matrix by 2 changes only its diagonal entries.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Scalar multiplication changes every entry. The diagonal has no special exemption in scalar arithmetic. Scaling only part of a stock table understates the remaining delivery quantities.

questions.prompt: Circle sectors: arc, area and perimeter — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

A non-full sector perimeter includes the arc and its two radii.
The perimeter of a sector equals its arc length.
questions.explanation: A non-full sector perimeter includes the arc and its two radii. The curved boundary is only one part of the region’s edge. Omitting radial sides understates material needed for its complete boundary.

questions.prompt: Composite areas and boundary lengths — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Subtracting a pond area means its boundary must also be subtracted from all edging.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Area subtraction and boundary counting are different operations.
questions.explanation: Area subtraction and boundary counting are different operations. A pond reduces grass area but adds an exposed inner edge if edging is required there. Choose boundaries from the practical task rather than copying area signs.

questions.prompt: Area and volume under similarity — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Similar enlargement by k gives area factor k² and volume factor k³.
Doubling every length doubles both area and volume.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Similar enlargement by k gives area factor k² and volume factor k³. For k=2 the factors are 4 and 8. Confusing the powers greatly understates covering or capacity requirements.

questions.prompt: Composite solids and tank capacity — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A tank filled to 80% of its height is always 80% full by volume.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Height fraction equals volume fraction only for constant cross-sectional area.
questions.explanation: Height fraction equals volume fraction only for constant cross-sectional area. A cone or curved cap has changing area with height. Use the stated volume fraction directly or calculate the partial solid from its geometry.

maa11-investigate.title: Planning a statistical investigation
maa11-investigate.unit: Unit 2 – Statistics, trigonometry and linear models
maa11-investigate.coverage: Lesson concept checks followed by related subject revision.

questions.prompt: Planning a statistical investigation — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Sample size reduces some random variability but does not automatically remove selection bias.
Increasing a convenience sample always removes selection bias.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Sample size reduces some random variability but does not automatically remove selection bias. An unrepresentative selection method can remain biased even with many observations. Improve the design and describe its limits before generalising.

questions.prompt: Slope, intercepts and straight-line graphs — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Numerical slope depends on coordinate changes and axis units.
A visually steeper line must have the larger slope even when graph scales differ.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Numerical slope depends on coordinate changes and axis units. Different scales can alter the visual angle without changing the underlying rate. Compare Δy/Δx in common units.

questions.prompt: Simultaneous linear equations and plan comparisons — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The intersection identifies equal cost at one usage level.
Finding an intersection proves the same plan is cheaper at every usage level.
questions.explanation: The intersection identifies equal cost at one usage level. Plans with different slopes can swap which is cheaper across it. Compare costs within the practical domain on both sides.

questions.prompt: Comparing group distributions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A smaller group median proves every member has a smaller value.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
A median comparison describes centres rather than every individual.
questions.explanation: A median comparison describes centres rather than every individual. Group distributions can overlap even when their medians differ. Use individual data or stronger bounds to establish an all-member statement.

questions.prompt: Building linear models from words — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Round down when a fractional maximum limits the number of complete affordable units.
An affordability maximum for complete items should always be rounded up.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Round down when a fractional maximum limits the number of complete affordable units. Rounding up can exceed the budget. Substitute the chosen integer to check the practical constraint.

questions.prompt: Triangle area from an included angle — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The angle must be included between the two chosen sides.
Any angle in the triangle can be used with any two sides in 0.5ab sinC.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: The angle must be included between the two chosen sides. The height interpretation relies on that side-angle pairing. Using a different angle produces the wrong perpendicular component.

questions.prompt: Mean, standard deviation and interpretation — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Adding a constant leaves deviations from the shifted mean unchanged.
Adding five to every value increases the standard deviation by five.
questions.explanation: Adding a constant leaves deviations from the shifted mean unchanged. The mean increases by five but SD does not. Spread and location respond differently to translations.

questions.prompt: Cosine rule for lengths and angles — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: The cross term is always added in the cosine rule.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The rule is c²=a²+b²−2ab cosC.
questions.explanation: The rule is c²=a²+b²−2ab cosC. When C is obtuse its cosine is negative, so subtracting that negative term increases c². Retain the formula’s minus sign and evaluate the cosine separately.

questions.prompt: Variable types, tables and displays — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Classification depends on the underlying variable, not rounding or digit format.
Any variable recorded as an integer is necessarily discrete numerical.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Classification depends on the underlying variable, not rounding or digit format. A rounded duration remains continuous and a numerical category code remains categorical. Choose a display from meaning and measurement rather than appearance.

questions.prompt: Bearings, route triangles and return directions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Bearings are measured clockwise from north.
A bearing is measured anticlockwise from east.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from north. North arrows and quadrants define the convention at every point. Using the wrong reference rotates or reflects the route and changes its angles.

questions.prompt: Angles of elevation and depression — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Total height includes the eye height when ground levels match.
The calculated height above the observer’s eye always equals the full tower height.
questions.explanation: Total height includes the eye height when ground levels match. The triangle’s vertical side begins at the observer’s horizontal eye line. Add the stated eye height after finding that vertical difference.

questions.prompt: Quartiles, outliers and modified box plots — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: The upper whisker always ends at Q3+1.5IQR.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The upper whisker ends at the largest observed value inside the upper fence.
questions.explanation: The upper whisker ends at the largest observed value inside the upper fence. The fence is a cutoff and may not be an observation. Use actual non-outlier values for whisker endpoints.

questions.prompt: Trigonometry in linked three-dimensional triangles — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: The horizontal distance is the ground diagonal between the two corners.
Use the courtyard width alone for elevation from a diagonally opposite corner.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: The horizontal distance is the ground diagonal between the two corners. Find it from both perpendicular ground dimensions. The elevation triangle must lie in the vertical plane through that diagonal.

questions.prompt: Normal probabilities and technology inputs — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
An interval probability subtracts the lower cumulative area from the upper.
For P(a
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: An interval probability subtracts the lower cumulative area from the upper. Both cumulative areas start at the far left, so addition double-counts that region. Sketching the requested interval helps verify the subtraction and tail direction.

questions.prompt: Heron’s rule and three-side area — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Heron’s s is half the perimeter.
Heron’s s is the full perimeter.
questions.explanation: Heron’s s is half the perimeter. The factors s−a, s−b and s−c use the semiperimeter. Using the full perimeter changes every factor and gives an incorrect area.

questions.prompt: Right-triangle ratios and inverse angles — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Opposite and adjacent are fixed labels regardless of the chosen acute angle.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Opposite and adjacent depend on the reference angle.
questions.explanation: Opposite and adjacent depend on the reference angle. Only hypotenuse has the same label for either acute angle. Relabel the known and unknown sides before choosing a ratio.

questions.prompt: Sine rule with opposite side–angle pairs — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A side pairs with the angle opposite it.
A side pairs with the angle touching it in the sine rule.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: A side pairs with the angle opposite it. Use the same opposite-pair convention in both fractions. An adjacent pairing can give a plausible numerical result that belongs to no valid triangle.

questions.prompt: Normal percentiles and central intervals — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
A central 80% interval uses the 10th and 90th percentiles.
The central 80% interval uses the 20th and 80th percentiles.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: A central 80% interval uses the 10th and 90th percentiles. Twenty percent lies outside and is split equally into the two tails. Subtract the percentile probabilities to check the enclosed probability.

questions.prompt: Normal models and standard scores — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
A z score of 2 means two standard deviations above the mean.

maa11-variables.title: Variable types, tables and displays
maa11-variables.unit: Unit 2 – Statistics, trigonometry and linear models
maa11-variables.coverage: Lesson concept checks followed by related subject revision.

questions.prompt: Variable types, tables and displays — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Classification depends on the underlying variable, not rounding or digit format.
Any variable recorded as an integer is necessarily discrete numerical.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Classification depends on the underlying variable, not rounding or digit format. A rounded duration remains continuous and a numerical category code remains categorical. Choose a display from meaning and measurement rather than appearance.

questions.prompt: Slope, intercepts and straight-line graphs — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Numerical slope depends on coordinate changes and axis units.
A visually steeper line must have the larger slope even when graph scales differ.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Numerical slope depends on coordinate changes and axis units. Different scales can alter the visual angle without changing the underlying rate. Compare Δy/Δx in common units.

questions.prompt: Simultaneous linear equations and plan comparisons — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The intersection identifies equal cost at one usage level.
Finding an intersection proves the same plan is cheaper at every usage level.
questions.explanation: The intersection identifies equal cost at one usage level. Plans with different slopes can swap which is cheaper across it. Compare costs within the practical domain on both sides.

questions.prompt: Comparing group distributions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A smaller group median proves every member has a smaller value.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
A median comparison describes centres rather than every individual.
questions.explanation: A median comparison describes centres rather than every individual. Group distributions can overlap even when their medians differ. Use individual data or stronger bounds to establish an all-member statement.

questions.prompt: Building linear models from words — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Round down when a fractional maximum limits the number of complete affordable units.
An affordability maximum for complete items should always be rounded up.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Round down when a fractional maximum limits the number of complete affordable units. Rounding up can exceed the budget. Substitute the chosen integer to check the practical constraint.

questions.prompt: Triangle area from an included angle — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The angle must be included between the two chosen sides.
Any angle in the triangle can be used with any two sides in 0.5ab sinC.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: The angle must be included between the two chosen sides. The height interpretation relies on that side-angle pairing. Using a different angle produces the wrong perpendicular component.

questions.prompt: Mean, standard deviation and interpretation — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Adding a constant leaves deviations from the shifted mean unchanged.
Adding five to every value increases the standard deviation by five.
questions.explanation: Adding a constant leaves deviations from the shifted mean unchanged. The mean increases by five but SD does not. Spread and location respond differently to translations.

questions.prompt: Cosine rule for lengths and angles — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: The cross term is always added in the cosine rule.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The rule is c²=a²+b²−2ab cosC.
questions.explanation: The rule is c²=a²+b²−2ab cosC. When C is obtuse its cosine is negative, so subtracting that negative term increases c². Retain the formula’s minus sign and evaluate the cosine separately.

questions.prompt: Bearings, route triangles and return directions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Bearings are measured clockwise from north.
A bearing is measured anticlockwise from east.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from north. North arrows and quadrants define the convention at every point. Using the wrong reference rotates or reflects the route and changes its angles.

questions.prompt: Angles of elevation and depression — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Total height includes the eye height when ground levels match.
The calculated height above the observer’s eye always equals the full tower height.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Total height includes the eye height when ground levels match. The triangle’s vertical side begins at the observer’s horizontal eye line. Add the stated eye height after finding that vertical difference.

questions.prompt: Quartiles, outliers and modified box plots — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The upper whisker ends at the largest observed value inside the upper fence.
The upper whisker always ends at Q3+1.5IQR.
questions.explanation: The upper whisker ends at the largest observed value inside the upper fence. The fence is a cutoff and may not be an observation. Use actual non-outlier values for whisker endpoints.

questions.prompt: Trigonometry in linked three-dimensional triangles — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Use the courtyard width alone for elevation from a diagonally opposite corner.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The horizontal distance is the ground diagonal between the two corners.
questions.explanation: The horizontal distance is the ground diagonal between the two corners. Find it from both perpendicular ground dimensions. The elevation triangle must lie in the vertical plane through that diagonal.

questions.prompt: Normal probabilities and technology inputs — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: An interval probability subtracts the lower cumulative area from the upper.

questions.explanation: An interval probability subtracts the lower cumulative area from the upper. Both cumulative areas start at the far left, so addition double-counts that region. Sketching the requested interval helps verify the subtraction and tail direction.

questions.prompt: Heron’s rule and three-side area — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Heron’s s is half the perimeter.
Heron’s s is the full perimeter.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Heron’s s is half the perimeter. The factors s−a, s−b and s−c use the semiperimeter. Using the full perimeter changes every factor and gives an incorrect area.

questions.prompt: Right-triangle ratios and inverse angles — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
Opposite and adjacent depend on the reference angle.
Opposite and adjacent are fixed labels regardless of the chosen acute angle.
questions.explanation: Opposite and adjacent depend on the reference angle. Only hypotenuse has the same label for either acute angle. Relabel the known and unknown sides before choosing a ratio.

questions.prompt: Sine rule with opposite side–angle pairs — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A side pairs with the angle touching it in the sine rule.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
A side pairs with the angle opposite it.
questions.explanation: A side pairs with the angle opposite it. Use the same opposite-pair convention in both fractions. An adjacent pairing can give a plausible numerical result that belongs to no valid triangle.

questions.prompt: Planning a statistical investigation — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Sample size reduces some random variability but does not automatically remove selection bias.
Increasing a convenience sample always removes selection bias.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Sample size reduces some random variability but does not automatically remove selection bias. An unrepresentative selection method can remain biased even with many observations. Improve the design and describe its limits before generalising.

questions.prompt: Normal percentiles and central intervals — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
A central 80% interval uses the 10th and 90th percentiles.
The central 80% interval uses the 20th and 80th percentiles.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: A central 80% interval uses the 10th and 90th percentiles. Twenty percent lies outside and is split equally into the two tails. Subtract the percentile probabilities to check the enclosed probability.

questions.prompt: Cosine rule for lengths and angles — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

questions.prompt: Variable types, tables and displays — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Bearings, route triangles and return directions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Angles of elevation and depression — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Quartiles, outliers and modified box plots — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

questions.prompt: Heron’s rule and three-side area — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Heron’s s is the full perimeter.

questions.prompt: Simultaneous linear equations and plan comparisons — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Comparing group distributions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Building linear models from words — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

Round down when a fractional maximum limits the number of complete affordable units.

questions.prompt: Triangle area from an included angle — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

The angle must be included between the two chosen sides.

questions.prompt: Mean, standard deviation and interpretation — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Adding a constant leaves deviations from the shifted mean unchanged.
Adding five to every value increases the standard deviation by five.
Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.
A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
questions.explanation: Adding a constant leaves deviations from the shifted mean unchanged. The mean increases by five but SD does not. Spread and location respond differently to translations.

questions.prompt: Cosine rule for lengths and angles — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
The rule is c²=a²+b²−2ab cosC.

questions.prompt: Variable types, tables and displays — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

questions.prompt: Angles of elevation and depression — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Quartiles, outliers and modified box plots — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.

questions.prompt: Normal probabilities and technology inputs — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
options: A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
An interval probability subtracts the lower cumulative area from the upper.

questions.prompt: Right-triangle ratios and inverse angles — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Sine rule with opposite side–angle pairs — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Planning a statistical investigation — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Normal percentiles and central intervals — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Normal models and standard scores — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.

questions.prompt: Continuous piecewise-linear tariffs — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

A worked example proves the rule for every possible situation.
A progressive second rate applies only to the excess block.

questions.prompt: Mean, standard deviation and interpretation — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.explanation: Classification depends on the underlying variable, not rounding or digit format. A rounded duration remains continuous and a numerical category code remains categorical. Choose a display from meaning and measurement rather than appearance.

questions.prompt: Bearings, route triangles and return directions — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

Changing measurement units changes every dimensionless ratio.

questions.prompt: Angles of elevation and depression — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?

questions.prompt: Quartiles, outliers and modified box plots — Which statement gives the correct reasoning for this lesson?
